name: Varanasi
tagline: Hinduism's holiest city, on the ghats of the Ganges
summary: One of the oldest living cities in the world, where Hindus come to bathe in the Ganges, pray at Kashi Vishwanath and, for many, to be cremated. Dawn boat rides past the ghats and the evening Ganga Aarti are unforgettable. Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon, is 10 km away.
seasonNote: October to March is pleasant; Dev Deepawali in November lights every ghat with lamps. April to June is very hot, and the monsoon (July to September) floods the lower ghats.
arrival: Fly to Varanasi airport (about 45 minutes from the ghats) from Delhi, Mumbai and other cities, or take an overnight train from Delhi (the Vande Bharat takes about 8 hours).
gettingAround: The old city is a maze of lanes best walked; cars cannot reach most ghats. Use e-rickshaws for longer hops and a boat to move along the river.
cashTip: UPI and cards work in hotels and bigger shops; carry small rupee notes for boats, chai and offerings.
foodTip: Varanasi is largely vegetarian: kachori and jalebi for breakfast, chaat in the evening, clay-cup lassi, and Banarasi paan to finish.
buyTip: Banarasi silk saris and scarves (buy from cooperatives, not touts), brass, wooden toys and rudraksha beads.
baseArea: Guesthouses on the ghats between Assi and Dashashwamedh

items.name: Dashashwamedh Ghat and the Ganga Aarti
items.summary: The main ghat, where priests perform the fire ritual of the Ganga Aarti every evening with lamps, bells and chanting.
items.expect: Huge crowds; arrive an hour early or watch from a boat.
items.tip: Book a boat for the aarti to see it from the river without the crush.
items.why: The defining ritual of Varanasi.
flow: Watch from the steps or a boat.

items.name: Sunrise boat ride along the ghats
items.summary: A rowing boat at dawn past bathers, priests, washing and morning prayers on 80 ghats.
items.expect: Agree the price and route before you set off.
items.tip: Start at Assi Ghat at first light and finish at Manikarnika.
items.why: The best way to see the city's daily life.
flow: Meet the boat at Assi Ghat before sunrise.

items.name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple
items.summary: The golden temple of Shiva, one of the most sacred in India, now reached by a broad new corridor from the river.
items.expect: Phones and bags must be left in lockers; long queues; non-Hindus may enter.
items.tip: Go early in the morning and leave everything but cash at your guesthouse.
items.why: The spiritual heart of Varanasi.
flow: Enter from the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor.

items.name: Manikarnika Ghat
items.summary: The main cremation ghat, where fires have burned day and night for centuries.
items.expect: No photos of cremations; touts may ask for 'donations', which you can decline.
items.tip: Watch respectfully from a boat or the upper steps.
items.why: A profound view of how Hindus see life and death.
flow: Approach by boat or the lanes.

items.name: Sarnath
items.summary: Where the Buddha gave his first sermon, with the great Dhamek Stupa, monastery ruins and the museum holding the Lion Capital of Ashoka.
items.expect: Calm and green; the museum is closed on Fridays.
items.tip: Go in the morning and see the museum's Lion Capital, India's national emblem.
items.why: One of the four holiest places in Buddhism.
flow: About 30 minutes by car or rickshaw.

items.name: Ramnagar Fort
items.summary: The 18th-century sandstone fort of the Maharajas of Benares, with a quirky museum of cars, palanquins and clocks.
items.expect: A faded but charming museum.
items.tip: Combine with a boat across the river at sunset.
items.why: The royal side of Varanasi.

items.name: Kachori Gali
items.summary: A lane near the ghats frying kachoris with spicy potato curry and hot jalebis from dawn.
items.expect: Standing room only; mornings are best.
items.tip: Follow kachori with a jalebi and a clay cup of chai.
items.why: The classic Varanasi breakfast.

items.name: Blue Lassi
items.summary: A tiny shop making thick lassi in clay cups with fruit toppings since 1925.
items.expect: A narrow lane on the way to Manikarnika; a short wait.
items.tip: Try the banana or pomegranate lassi.
items.why: The most famous lassi in the city.
flow: Find it in the lane above Manikarnika.
Sit on the bench and wait.

items.name: Deena Chaat Bhandar
items.summary: A busy chaat shop known for tamatar chaat, tangy tomato with spices, and aloo tikki.
items.expect: Crowded in the evening.
items.tip: Order tamatar chaat, a Varanasi speciality.
items.why: The city's best-loved street snack.
flow: Walk up from the evening aarti.

name: Amritsar
tagline: The Golden Temple, Sikhism's holiest shrine
summary: Amritsar is home to the Golden Temple, the holiest site of Sikhism, open to people of every faith and feeding up to 100,000 people a day in its free community kitchen. The city also holds the Jallianwala Bagh memorial, the Partition Museum, and the nightly border ceremony at Attari–Wagah.
seasonNote: October to March is best, though December and January bring fog and cold nights. May and June pass 40°C. Guru Nanak's birthday (November) and Diwali light up the temple.
arrival: Fly to Amritsar (about 30 minutes from the temple) or take the Shatabdi or Vande Bharat train from Delhi (about 6 hours).
gettingAround: The old city around the temple is pedestrian; use cycle or e-rickshaws. Book a taxi or shared jeep for the border ceremony.
cashTip: UPI and cards are common; carry small notes for rickshaws and food stalls.
foodTip: Punjabi food at its richest: Amritsari kulcha with chole, dal makhani, fish fry and thick lassi. The Golden Temple's langar is free for all.
buyTip: Phulkari embroidery, juttis (embroidered shoes), papad and wadi spices, and kada steel bracelets.
baseArea: Hotels around the Golden Temple and Heritage Street

items.name: Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib)
items.summary: The gilded temple in the middle of its sacred pool, with hymns sung from dawn to late night and a free kitchen for everyone.
items.expect: Open to all faiths, around the clock. Remove shoes, wash your feet and cover your head; scarves are lent at the gate. No alcohol or tobacco.
items.tip: Come twice: before dawn for the procession that brings the holy book in, and after dark when the temple glows.
items.why: One of the most welcoming and beautiful holy places in the world.
flow: Leave shoes at the free deposit.
Walk the marble path around the pool, then the langar hall.

items.name: Jallianwala Bagh
items.summary: The garden memorial to the 1919 massacre, when British troops fired on a peaceful crowd, with bullet marks still in the walls.
items.expect: A quiet garden and small gallery; free.
items.tip: Pair it with the Partition Museum a few minutes away.
items.why: A turning point in India's road to independence.
flow: Memorial, the martyrs' well, the gallery.

items.name: Partition Museum
items.summary: A moving museum of the 1947 Partition of India, told through survivors' stories and belongings.
items.expect: Closed on Mondays; allow two hours.
items.tip: Listen to the oral histories in the last galleries.
items.why: The best museum of Partition anywhere.

items.name: Attari–Wagah border ceremony
items.summary: The nightly lowering of the flags at the India–Pakistan border, a loud show of high kicks, drums and cheering crowds.
items.expect: Arrive two hours early; no bags allowed; ID needed.
items.tip: Foreigners have a separate seating section closer to the gate; bring your passport.
items.why: Theatre and national pride like nowhere else.
flow: Security, seats, then the ceremony before sunset.

items.name: Gobindgarh Fort
items.summary: An 18th-century fort turned heritage park, with museums and an evening light show on Punjab's history.
items.expect: Busier in the evening.
items.tip: Go for the evening show and Punjabi food stalls.
items.why: A lively introduction to Sikh and Punjabi history.
flow: Taxi or rickshaw from the old city.

items.name: Durgiana Temple
items.summary: A Hindu temple set in a sacred tank, built in the style of the Golden Temple.
items.expect: Shoes off; calm compared with the Golden Temple.
items.tip: Visit in the evening when the lamps are lit.
items.why: Shows Amritsar's shared Hindu and Sikh heritage.

items.name: Golden Temple langar
items.summary: The free community kitchen where volunteers serve dal, roti and kheer to everyone, seated together on the floor.
items.expect: Free; cover your head; sit in rows on mats.
items.tip: Offer an hour of help peeling garlic or washing plates afterwards.
items.why: The world's largest free kitchen, run by volunteers.
flow: Collect a plate at the hall entrance.
Sit in line and hold out your hands for roti.

items.name: Kesar Da Dhaba
items.summary: A century-old dhaba in the old city lanes, famous for slow-cooked dal and rich parathas.
items.expect: Simple, packed and vegetarian.
items.tip: Order the dal makhani with lachha paratha and finish with phirni.
items.why: A legend of Punjabi home-style cooking.
flow: Find it in the lanes near the temple.

items.name: Amritsari kulcha stalls
items.summary: Crisp stuffed kulcha from clay ovens, brushed with butter and served with chole.
items.expect: Morning and lunch; quick service.
items.tip: Order the mixed kulcha and a sweet lassi.
items.why: Amritsar's signature dish.

name: Rishikesh · Haridwar
tagline: The yoga capital, where the Ganges leaves the Himalaya
summary: Rishikesh sits where the Ganges rushes out of the Himalayan foothills, with ashrams, suspension bridges, evening aartis and the ashram where the Beatles stayed in 1968. It is a centre for yoga and meditation, and for white-water rafting. Holy Haridwar, a short drive downstream, holds one of India's great river ceremonies.
seasonNote: February to April and September to November are best; the International Yoga Festival is in March. Rafting stops in the monsoon (July and August), when landslides close roads.
arrival: Fly to Dehradun's Jolly Grant airport (about 40 minutes), or take a train from Delhi to Haridwar (about 4.5 hours) and a taxi on.
gettingAround: Walk between the ashrams and bridges; shared tempos and taxis link Rishikesh, Tapovan and Haridwar.
cashTip: UPI is widely used; carry cash for small cafés, temples and rafting operators.
foodTip: Rishikesh is a vegetarian, alcohol-free holy town: thalis, Ayurvedic cafés, chai and fresh juices.
buyTip: Yoga mats and clothes, rudraksha beads, singing bowls and Ayurvedic oils.
baseArea: Tapovan and Laxman Jhula for cafés and yoga, Swarg Ashram for ashrams

connections.note: Train to Haridwar, then 45 minutes by taxi.

items.name: Laxman Jhula and Ram Jhula
items.summary: The iron suspension bridges over the green Ganges, lined with temples, cafés and the 13-storey Trayambakeshwar temple.
items.expect: Laxman Jhula itself is closed for safety, with a new bridge beside it; Ram Jhula is open.
items.tip: Walk between the two bridges along the river in the evening.
items.why: The picture-postcard view of Rishikesh.
flow: Walk the riverbank to Ram Jhula.

items.name: Ganga Aarti at Parmarth Niketan
items.summary: A riverside evening ceremony of song, fire and prayer at one of Rishikesh's largest ashrams.
items.expect: Free and open to all; sit on the steps by the river.
items.tip: Arrive 30 minutes before sunset for a seat near the front.
items.why: A gentler, more musical aarti than Varanasi's.
flow: Cross Ram Jhula to Swarg Ashram.

items.name: Beatles Ashram (Chaurasi Kutia)
items.summary: The overgrown ashram of Maharishi Mahesh Yogi where the Beatles stayed in 1968, now covered in murals.
items.expect: Ruins in the forest; entry fee for foreigners.
items.tip: Climb into the meditation domes and look for the Beatles murals.
items.why: A strange and beautiful piece of music history.

items.name: White-water rafting on the Ganges
items.summary: Grade II to IV rapids on the Ganges from Shivpuri back to Rishikesh, with cliff jumping and a beach stop.
items.expect: Licensed operators only; season runs October to June.
items.tip: The 16 km Shivpuri run is the classic half-day trip.
items.why: Some of the best rafting in India.

items.name: Neelkanth Mahadev Temple
items.summary: A Shiva temple in the forested hills where, by legend, Shiva drank poison to save the world.
items.expect: A winding road or a long forest hike; busy in the monsoon pilgrimage.
items.tip: Hike up the old forest path in the morning and take a jeep back.
items.why: Forest views and a revered temple.
flow: Shared jeep or hike from Ram Jhula.
Temple, then tea at the top.

items.name: Har Ki Pauri, Haridwar
items.summary: Haridwar's holiest ghat, where thousands float leaf boats of flowers and lamps on the Ganges at the evening aarti.
items.expect: Very crowded; watch your bags.
items.tip: Buy a leaf-boat diya and float it at sunset.
items.why: One of the great river ceremonies of India, and a Kumbh Mela site.

items.name: Chotiwala
items.summary: A Rishikesh institution since 1958, serving vegetarian thalis by the river.
items.expect: Simple and busy; look for the doorman with the painted face.
items.tip: Order the special thali.
items.why: The classic Rishikesh meal.

items.name: Tapovan cafés
items.summary: Rooftop cafés above the river serving smoothie bowls, Israeli and Tibetan food and Ayurvedic thalis.
items.expect: Relaxed, with yoga students lingering for hours.
items.tip: Pick a rooftop with a river view for sunset.
items.why: The social life of yoga town.

items.name: Haridwar sweets and puri
items.summary: Bazaar stalls frying puri with potato curry, kachori and hot jalebi near Har Ki Pauri.
items.expect: Busy, cheap, vegetarian.
items.tip: Eat before the evening aarti.
items.why: The pilgrim's meal in Haridwar.

name: Mumbai
tagline: India's city of dreams, from colonial Fort to Bollywood
summary: India's biggest and richest city, packed onto islands in the Arabian Sea. Gothic railway stations and Art Deco seafronts sit beside markets, temples and the island caves of Elephanta. Eat street food on Juhu and Chowpatty beaches, walk Marine Drive at dusk, and feel the energy of the film capital of India.
seasonNote: November to February is dry and warm. The monsoon (June to September) is spectacular but floods streets. Ganesh Chaturthi in August or September is the city's biggest festival.
arrival: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport is 45 to 90 minutes from South Mumbai depending on traffic; the coastal road has cut times.
gettingAround: Local trains are fast but packed (use first class or avoid rush hour); metro lines are growing. Taxis and Uber everywhere; rickshaws only in the suburbs.
cashTip: UPI and cards are everywhere; carry some cash for street food and taxis.
foodTip: Vada pav, pav bhaji and bhel puri on the beaches, Parsi café classics like berry pulao, and seafood from the Konkan coast.
buyTip: Colaba Causeway for clothes and souvenirs, Crawford Market for spices, and Chor Bazaar for antiques.
baseArea: Colaba and Fort for sights; Bandra for nightlife

connections.note: Vande Bharat or Konkan Railway along the coast.

items.name: Gateway of India and Colaba
items.summary: The 1924 harbour arch facing the Taj Mahal Palace hotel, where boats leave for Elephanta.
items.expect: Crowded and lively; security checks.
items.tip: Come early morning for photos without the crowds, then take the Elephanta ferry.
items.why: Mumbai's landmark.

items.name: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus
items.summary: A riotous Victorian Gothic railway station and World Heritage Site, still used by millions every day.
items.expect: A heritage gallery runs guided tours inside.
items.tip: See it lit up at night from across the road.
items.why: One of the great railway buildings of the world.

items.name: Elephanta Caves
items.summary: Rock-cut cave temples to Shiva on an island in the harbour, with a giant three-headed sculpture.
items.expect: One-hour ferry each way; steps up to the caves; closed on Mondays.
items.tip: Take the first ferry from the Gateway to beat the heat.
items.why: Masterpieces of Indian rock-cut sculpture.
flow: Ferry from the Gateway of India.

items.name: Marine Drive
items.summary: The curving seafront promenade lined with Art Deco buildings, known as the Queen's Necklace at night.
items.expect: Joggers at dawn, families at dusk.
items.tip: Walk to Chowpatty Beach at sunset for bhel puri.
items.why: Mumbai's favourite evening walk.

items.name: CSMVS museum
items.summary: Mumbai's main museum, in an Indo-Saracenic building, with sculpture, miniature paintings and decorative arts.
items.expect: Allow two hours; audio guide included.
items.tip: Wander Kala Ghoda's galleries and cafés afterwards.
items.why: The best overview of Indian art in the city.

items.name: Haji Ali Dargah
items.summary: A white mosque and tomb on an islet, reached by a causeway that floods at high tide.
items.expect: Open to all faiths; cover your head.
items.tip: Check the tide times and go at low tide.
items.why: One of Mumbai's most loved shrines.

items.name: Juhu and Chowpatty street food
items.summary: Beachside stalls serving vada pav, pav bhaji, bhel puri and kulfi.
items.expect: Busiest at sunset and weekends.
items.tip: Pick stalls with filtered-water signs and long queues.
items.why: Mumbai's street food at its best.

items.name: Britannia & Co.
items.summary: A 1923 Parsi-Irani café famous for its berry pulao and caramel custard.
items.expect: Lunch only, closed on Sundays.
items.tip: Order the berry chicken pulao.
items.why: A last link to Mumbai's Irani cafés.

items.name: Leopold Cafe
items.summary: A Colaba café and bar since 1871, busy with travellers and locals.
items.expect: Loud and lively; a broad menu.
items.tip: Go for a beer and snacks after the Gateway.
items.why: A Mumbai institution.

name: Goa
tagline: Beaches, Portuguese churches and fish curry
summary: India's smallest state mixes palm-lined beaches with Portuguese-era churches, spice farms and a laid-back, Catholic-Hindu culture. North Goa has the party beaches and markets, the south is quieter, and Old Goa's churches are a World Heritage Site.
seasonNote: November to March is beach season, with Christmas and New Year the busiest and priciest. The monsoon (June to September) closes most beach shacks but turns the hills green.
arrival: Two airports: Dabolim near Vasco and Mopa in the north. Trains from Mumbai run along the Konkan coast (8 to 10 hours).
gettingAround: Rent a scooter or hire a taxi; the GoaMiles app sets fixed fares. Buses link the main towns.
cashTip: Cards work in hotels and restaurants; carry cash for shacks, markets and scooter hire.
foodTip: Goan fish curry with rice, prawn balchão, pork vindaloo and xacuti, washed down with feni or kokum.
buyTip: Cashews, feni, spices, azulejo-style tiles and the Wednesday Anjuna flea market.
baseArea: Panaji (Panjim) for culture, Assagao and Anjuna for the north, Palolem for the south

items.name: Old Goa churches and Basilica of Bom Jesus
items.summary: The 16th-century basilica holding the body of St Francis Xavier, beside Sé Cathedral and other churches of the former Portuguese capital.
items.expect: Modest dress; free entry.
items.tip: Visit early before the tour buses, and see Sé Cathedral across the road.
items.why: A World Heritage Site and the heart of Goa's history.
flow: Sé Cathedral and the Church of St Francis of Assisi.

items.name: Fontainhas, Panaji
items.summary: Panaji's Latin Quarter of colourful Portuguese houses, chapels and tiny bakeries.
items.expect: Quiet residential lanes; respect residents.
items.tip: Walk at golden hour, ending at the Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception.
items.why: The prettiest neighbourhood in Goa.
flow: Start at the São Sebastião chapel.
Wander the lanes to the church.

items.name: Anjuna and Vagator beaches
items.summary: Rocky coves, cliff-top cafés and the famous Wednesday flea market of North Goa.
items.expect: Lively in season; strong currents in places.
items.tip: Visit the flea market on Wednesday, then sunset at Chapora Fort.
items.why: The spirit of Goa's hippie history.
flow: Sunset at Chapora Fort above Vagator.

items.name: Fort Aguada
items.summary: A 17th-century Portuguese fort and lighthouse at the mouth of the Mandovi River.
items.expect: Short visit; views over the sea.
items.tip: Go in the late afternoon and stay for sunset.
items.why: Goa's best-preserved fort.

items.name: Palolem Beach
items.summary: A crescent of sand backed by palms, calm water and beach huts in quiet South Goa.
items.expect: Calm swimming in season; silent-headphone parties some nights.
items.tip: Kayak to Butterfly Beach in the morning.
items.why: The most beautiful beach in Goa.
flow: About 1.5 hours by car from Panaji.

items.name: Dudhsagar Falls
items.summary: A 310 m four-tiered waterfall in the jungle on the Karnataka border.
items.expect: Reached by jeep safari; may close in heavy monsoon.
items.tip: Combine with a spice farm visit near Ponda.
items.why: One of India's tallest waterfalls.

items.name: Ritz Classic
items.summary: A Panaji favourite for Goan fish curry thali and fried fish.
items.expect: Queues at lunch.
items.tip: Order the fish thali with kingfish.
items.why: The classic Goan lunch.

items.name: Viva Panjim
items.summary: A family-run restaurant in a Fontainhas house, serving Goan-Portuguese dishes.
items.expect: Small and homely.
items.tip: Try the pork vindaloo and bebinca.
items.why: Home-style Goan cooking in the Latin Quarter.

items.name: Beach shacks
items.summary: Seasonal shacks on the sand serving grilled fish, prawn curry and cold beer.
items.expect: Open November to May.
items.tip: Choose your fish from the display and ask for it tandoori-style.
items.why: The essential Goa evening.
flow: Order the catch of the day.
